title: Testing and data
summary: How to design clean tests, size them sensibly and read results without being fooled by luck. You leave with written kill and scale rules, a lean dashboard and a weekly review habit.

lessons.title: Noise: why early numbers lie
objectives: By the end you can explain what noise is and why it shows up in every campaign.
You can use a rough range to judge whether a gap between two ads could be luck.
You can tell a random swing apart from a real problem such as broken tracking.

steps.h: Results wobble even when nothing changes
steps.p: Run the same ad twice with the same budget and you will get different results. People see ads at random moments. Some are busy, some are ready to act. That random wobble is called noise. Your job is to tell real differences from noise before you move money.

d.s: Randomness is part of every campaign

steps.say: Here's something that surprises most beginners. Run the same ad twice, with the same budget, and you'll get different results. Why? Because people see ads at random moments. Some are busy, some are ready to act. That random wobble is called noise. It's part of every campaign, and it never goes away. Your job is to tell real differences from noise before you move any money.

steps.p: A signal is a difference that keeps showing up because something real caused it. Noise is a difference that appears and then vanishes. The danger is acting on noise: killing a good ad after a bad morning, or scaling a weak one after a lucky day.

a.title: Noise
items: Shows up on one day only

steps.say: Look at the two columns. Noise shows up on one day only, flips when you wait, is built on one to three conversions, and has no clear reason behind it. A signal holds across several days, gets clearer with more data, is built on many conversions, and has a believable cause. The real danger is acting on noise. That means killing a good ad after a bad morning, or scaling a weak one after a lucky day.

steps.p: Flip a fair coin ten times. Getting seven heads happens often, yet nobody would say the coin prefers heads. Conversions behave the same way. With small numbers, lopsided results happen by chance all the time, so an early lead between two ads means very little.
steps.more: Seven or more heads out of ten happens about 17% of the time with a fair coin, so roughly one run in six. Now picture two copies of the same ad, each expected to bring 1 or 2 sign-ups on $20. One getting 3 and the other getting 0 is an ordinary outcome. If you killed Ad B on that evidence you would be throwing away an ad that is exactly as good as Ad A.

d.text: Example: two identical ads, $20 each. Ad A gets 3 sign-ups and Ad B gets 0. With counts this small, chance alone can easily produce that gap.

steps.p: Clicks arrive in hundreds. Deposits arrive in ones and twos. The further down the funnel you look, the smaller the count and the bigger the wobble. That is why click-through rate settles fast while cost per FTD can swing hard for days.
steps.more: Example funnel. With 750 clicks, one extra click barely moves CTR (from 1.50% to 1.502%). With 6 FTDs, one extra FTD changes cost per FTD by about 14%. If spend is $180, cost per FTD is $30 at 6 FTDs and about $25.70 at 7. One person decided that swing.
steps.say: Follow the funnel down. Fifty thousand impressions, seven hundred and fifty clicks, one hundred and fifty joins, and just six F T Ds, first time deposits. Clicks arrive in hundreds, deposits in ones and twos. The further down you look, the smaller the count and the bigger the wobble. One extra click barely moves C T R, your click through rate. But one extra F T D changes cost per F T D by about fourteen percent. On one hundred and eighty dollars of spend, that's thirty dollars at six, and about twenty five dollars seventy at seven. One person decided that swing.

steps.h: A rough range for any count
steps.p: Here is a simple intuition, not an exact law. For a count of conversions, the natural wobble is around the square root of that count. Doubling it gives a rough range where the true figure could sit. It is enough to stop you from overreacting.
steps.more: This comes from how random counts behave (statisticians call them Poisson counts). It is a rough guide only, and it assumes nothing else changed, such as budget, audience, offer or tracking. Use it to ask one question: could this gap be luck? It is never proof that a gap is real, and you should not quote it to two decimal places.
steps.say: Here's a simple intuition, not an exact law. For any count of conversions, the natural wobble is around the square root of that count. Take the count, plus or minus two times its square root, and you get a rough range where the true figure could sit. Statisticians call these Poisson counts. It's a rough guide only, and it assumes nothing else changed. Use it to ask one question: could this gap be luck? It's never proof that a gap is real.

steps.h: What the rough range looks like
steps.p: The table shows how wide the rough range is at different counts. Small counts have huge ranges compared with their size. At 4 conversions the true figure could be anywhere from almost zero to double. At 100 it is about 20% either side.
steps.say: This table shows how wide the rough range gets. If you saw four conversions, the square root is two, so the range is zero to eight. At nine, it's three to fifteen. At twenty five, fifteen to thirty five. And at one hundred, eighty to one hundred and twenty. Notice how small counts have huge ranges compared with their size. At four, the true figure could be almost zero or double. At one hundred, it's about twenty percent either side.

steps.p: Example: Ad A has 9 FTDs and Ad B has 4 on the same spend. A looks more than twice as good. But A's rough range is 3 to 15 and B's is 0 to 8. The ranges overlap a lot, so the gap may be luck. Keep both running a little longer.
steps.more: Example. 9 ± 2 × 3 gives 3 to 15. 4 ± 2 × 2 gives 0 to 8. When ranges overlap this much, the honest answer is that you do not know yet. If after more spend A has 30 FTDs (range about 19 to 41) and B has 12 (range about 5 to 19), the ranges barely touch and you can act with more confidence.
steps.say: Let's compare two ads honestly. In this example, Ad A has nine F T Ds and Ad B has four, on the same spend. A looks more than twice as good. But look at the bars. A's rough range is three to fifteen, and B's is zero to eight. They overlap a lot, so the gap may be luck, and the honest answer is that you don't know yet. Keep both running a little longer. If A later reaches thirty and B twelve, the ranges barely touch, and you can act with more confidence.

steps.p: Track cost per result day by day and a pattern appears. The first days swing hard, then the line calms down as data piles up. Decisions made on day one are often reversed by day five. Waiting for the line to settle is part of the method.
steps.more: Example, cumulative cost per lead. On day 1 Ad B looked four times cheaper than Ad A. By day 7 the two sit within a few dollars of each other. A buyer who killed Ad A on day 1 would have lost an ad that ended up slightly cheaper.

steps.p: A result that is unusually good today is likely to look more ordinary tomorrow. This is called regression to the mean. It explains why the ad you scaled after one great day often disappoints, and why a cold ad sometimes recovers with no changes.
d: Lucky day|often followed by an average one
Bad day|often followed by a recovery
Scaling on one day|you buy the average, not the peak
steps.say: A result that's unusually good today is likely to look more ordinary tomorrow. This is called regression to the mean. Look at the cards. A lucky day is often followed by an average one. A bad day is often followed by a recovery. If you scale on one day, you buy the average, not the peak. The fix is to judge several days together. That's why the ad you scaled after one great day often disappoints.

steps.p: Not every swing is luck. Some changes have real causes, and you should look for them before you shrug. Check these first when numbers move sharply, because they need action rather than patience.
d: Offer paused or capped by the network
Budget, bid or audience was edited
Payday, holiday or big match day
steps.say: But not every swing is luck. Some changes have real causes, and they need action, not patience. When numbers move sharply, check these first. Has tracking or the postback stopped firing? Was the offer paused or capped by the network? Was the ad rejected or the account limited? Did someone edit the budget, bid or audience? Or is it payday, a holiday or a big match day? Look for these before you shrug and call it noise.

steps.p: Checking results every hour is fine. Acting on them every hour is the problem. Each time you look and react, you give noise another chance to fool you. Look as often as you like, but only make decisions at the checkpoints you set before launch.

d.text: Set decision checkpoints in advance, for example each time spend reaches another 1x of your target CPA. Between checkpoints, act only on broken tracking or policy problems.

steps.say: Here's a simple habit. Look often, decide rarely. Checking results every hour is fine. Acting on them every hour is the problem, because each reaction gives noise another chance to fool you. Read the warning. Set decision checkpoints in advance, for example each time spend reaches another one times your target C P A, your cost per acquisition. Between checkpoints, act only on broken tracking or policy problems.

steps.h: The rule card is your noise filter
steps.p: The rule card in the Budget and kill rules module is built to resist noise. A zero kills only at 2 × target CPA. CPA kills only once spend reaches 3 × target. Scaling needs 3 or more network-confirmed conversions at CPA ≤ 0.8 × target. Below those lines the answer is Hold. Starting rules; adapt them.

d.text: Example: target $25. $20 spent, 0 FTDs: Hold, the kill line is $50. $55 spent, 0 FTDs, network confirms: Kill.

steps.say: The rule card from the Budget and kill rules module is built to resist noise. A zero kills only at two times target C P A. A C P A kill only happens once spend reaches three times target. Scaling needs three or more network-confirmed conversions, at a C P A of point eight times target or less. Below those lines, the answer is hold. Look at the example. Target twenty five dollars. Twenty dollars spent with zero F T Ds: hold, because the kill line is fifty. Fifty five spent, zero F T Ds, network confirms: kill. These are starting rules, so adapt them.

steps.h: Lab: a zero after one day
steps.p: Copy B above had zero results. Suppose those were FTDs and your target is $25. Apply the rule card instead of your gut, then press check to see the working.
steps.more: Answer: hold. $20 ÷ $25 = 0.8 × target, well under the 2 × zero-conversion kill line of $50. With counts this small, a zero is what chance often looks like. Wait for the next checkpoint.

Copy B spent twenty dollars in one day, with zero network-confirmed F T Ds. Should you kill, hold or scale? Don't go with your gut. Apply the rule card. Pause and try it, then check your answer.

steps.p: Every one of these mistakes comes from treating a small count as a verdict. They feel like quick, decisive management. In practice they kill good ads, feed lucky ones and make next week's data even noisier.

a.title: Mistakes
items: Editing ad sets every few hours

b.title: Fixes
items: Scale on 3+ conversions and the rule card

steps.say: These are the common noise mistakes. Killing after one bad morning. Scaling after one great day. Calling three conversions against one a win. And editing ad sets every few hours. Now the fixes on the right. Decide only at planned checkpoints. Scale on three or more conversions and the rule card. Check the rough ranges first. And look often, act rarely. Every mistake treats a small count as a verdict. It feels decisive, but it kills good ads and feeds lucky ones.

steps.p: Time alone does not make a result trustworthy. Ten days with two conversions tells you less than one day with forty. Count how many conversions sit behind a number, then decide how much weight it deserves. Small counts are hints, never verdicts.

d.s: Rough guide: under 10 conversions, treat it as a hint

steps.say: Here's the big idea to take away. Time alone doesn't make a result trustworthy. Ten days with two conversions tells you less than one day with forty. So count how many conversions sit behind a number, then decide how much weight it deserves. As a rough guide, under ten conversions, treat it as a hint. Small counts are hints, never verdicts. More conversions means more trust.

takeaways: Noise is random wobble; it is largest when conversion counts are small.
A rough range of count ± 2 × √count tells you whether a gap could be luck.
Rule out real causes such as broken tracking before you blame noise, and decide only at planned checkpoints.

glossary.def: Random variation in results that has no real cause. It is biggest when counts are small.
A difference in results that holds up over time because something real caused it.
Count plus or minus two times its square root. A quick way to see how much a count could wobble by chance.
The tendency of unusually good or bad results to be followed by more ordinary ones.
A point set before launch, often a spend level, where you are allowed to make a decision.

quiz.q: Two identical ads each spend $20. One gets 3 sign-ups and the other gets 0. What is the most honest reading?
options: The first ad is clearly better
The gap could easily be chance
The second ad has broken tracking
The first ad should get all the budget
quiz.why: With counts this small, a 3 to 0 split happens by chance often. You need more data before calling a winner.

quiz.q: Which metric settles fastest as spend grows?
quiz.why: CTR is built on hundreds or thousands of clicks, so one extra event barely moves it. Deposit-based numbers rest on small counts and swing more.

quiz.q: Using the rough range rule, what range fits a count of 25?
quiz.why: The square root of 25 is 5. Two times 5 is 10, so 25 ± 10 gives 15 to 35.

quiz.q: Cost per FTD jumps sharply overnight and the network shows zero FTDs while joins look normal. What do you check first?
options: Whether the ad needs a new hook
Whether the budget is too low
Whether the postback and offer are working
quiz.why: A sudden drop to zero with normal joins points to a real cause, such as a broken postback or paused offer. Rule that out before blaming noise.

quiz.q: You scaled an ad after its best day ever and the next three days were average. What most likely happened?
quiz.why: An unusually good day tends to be followed by ordinary ones. Scaling on one peak day buys the average, not the peak.

lessons.title: Designing a clean test
objectives: By the end you can write a hypothesis with a change, an expected result and a reason.
You can set up a test that changes one variable against a control.
You can choose the success metric and decision rule before launch.

steps.h: A test is a question with a budget
steps.p: A test answers one question, such as: does a talking-head video beat a screen recording for this offer? Without a clear question you are just spending and watching. Write the question down before you build anything, and give it its own budget.
steps.say: A test is a question with a budget. It answers one question, such as: does a talking-head video beat a screen recording for this offer? Without a clear question, you're just spending and watching. So write the question down before you build anything, and give it its own budget. One question per test, written down before launch.

steps.p: Every good test follows the same loop. You predict what will happen, build the smallest test that can check it, run it to a planned amount of data, read it with honest rules, and record the outcome so the next test starts smarter.
steps.say: Every good test follows the same loop. Follow the flow on screen. Hypothesis: you predict what will happen. Design: you build the smallest test that can check it. Run: you run it to a planned amount of data. Read: you read it with honest rules. And record: you write down the outcome, so the next test starts smarter. Then the loop begins again.

steps.p: A useful hypothesis names the change, the expected result and the reason. The reason matters because it tells you what to try next, whether you win or lose. Vague guesses like video will do better give you nothing to build on.
steps.more: Example hypothesis: if we open the video with a person speaking Pidgin instead of a text card, cost per join will drop by at least 20%, because people stop scrolling for a familiar voice. If it wins, the next test might try other local languages. If it loses, you have learned that the voice was not the barrier, and you look at the offer or the angle instead.
steps.say: A useful hypothesis has three parts. If we change X, we expect Y, because of Z. Here's an example. If we open the video with a person speaking Pidgin instead of a text card, cost per join will drop by at least twenty percent, because people stop scrolling for a familiar voice. The reason matters most. If it wins, you might try other local languages next. If it loses, you've learned the voice wasn't the barrier, so you look at the offer or the angle instead.

steps.h: Change one variable at a time
steps.p: If you change the hook, the audience and the landing page at once and results improve, you will not know which change helped. Change one thing, keep everything else the same, and the result points to a cause you can reuse.
steps.say: Change one variable at a time. Look at the messy test on the left: new hook and new audience, different budgets, launched on different days, two landers mixed in. If results improve, which change helped? You can't tell. Now the clean test on the right: only the hook changes, equal budgets, same start time and schedule, same lander and offer. Change one thing, keep everything else the same, and the result points to a cause you can reuse.

steps.p: Some variables move results far more than others. Test the big levers first: offer and geo, then angle, then hook. Button text and small copy edits rarely matter until the big pieces are right. The order below is a rough guide that varies by vertical.
steps.say: Some variables move results far more than others. Look at the bars. Offer and geo is the biggest lever. Then angle, which is large. Then the hook, the first three seconds, also large. Format is medium. Body copy is small, and button text is tiny. So test the big levers first. Button text and small copy edits rarely matter until the big pieces are right. This order is a rough guide, and it varies by vertical.

steps.p: Every test needs a control: your current best version, left untouched. Variants are the new versions you compare with it. Without a control you cannot tell whether a change helped or whether the whole market moved that week.
d: Winner|beats control on the agreed metric
steps.say: Every test needs a control. Look at the cards. The control is your current best version, left unchanged. A variant is one change from the control. The baseline is the control's usual numbers. And the winner is whatever beats the control on the agreed metric. Why does the control matter? Without one, you can't tell whether a change helped, or whether the whole market moved that week.

steps.p: Decide before launch which number settles the test. Pick the metric closest to money that still gives you enough data in your budget. For a creative test that is often cost per join or cost per lead, checked later against deposits.
steps.say: Decide before launch which number settles the test. Pick the metric closest to money that still gives you enough data in your budget. Look at the table. For a hook test, use hook rate or C T R, click through rate, then check cost per lead later. For an angle test, cost per lead or join, then check cost per F T D, first time deposit. For audiences, cost per F T D, then deposit quality. For a lander, its conversion rate. For a geo, cost per F T D against payout, then holds and approvals.

steps.p: Good hypotheses come from somewhere. Before you write one, look at which angles and formats other advertisers in your geo keep running for weeks; long-running ads are often working. Use them to learn angles, never to copy someone's creative.

d.why: See which angles and formats keep running in your geo, so your next hypothesis starts from evidence.

steps.say: Good hypotheses come from somewhere. Before you write one, look at which angles and formats other advertisers in your geo keep running for weeks, because long-running ads are often working. That's what Spyvoo, shown here, helps with. steps.p: Ads inside one ad set let the platform choose, so spend often goes unevenly. Separate ad sets with equal budgets, or the platform's built-in A/B test tool, give a fairer split. Names and tools change; check the current Ads Manager.
steps.more: Letting the platform pick inside one ad set is not useless. It is a cheap way to screen many hooks and find candidates, because the platform quickly drifts toward ads it expects to perform. The catch is that ads it ignored early never got a fair chance. Use that kind of screening to build a shortlist, then confirm the shortlist with a fair split.
steps.say: Now, building a fair split. When several ads sit inside one ad set, the platform chooses, and spend often goes unevenly. Ads it ignored early never get a fair chance. That screening is still a cheap way to build a shortlist of hooks. But to confirm, follow the flow. Duplicate the control ad set. Change one thing. Set equal budgets. Launch together. Then wait for the checkpoint. Separate ad sets, or the platform's built-in A B test tool, give a fairer split. Names and tools change, so check the current Ads Manager.

steps.p: Small details can break a test without you noticing. Run through this list before launch so the only difference between control and variant is the one you chose to test.
d: Same landing page and offer link
steps.say: Small details can break a test without you noticing. Before launch, run through this list. Same audience and placements. Same budget and bid strategy. Same start time and schedule. Same landing page and offer link. And tracking checked on both. The goal is simple. The only difference between control and variant should be the one you chose to test.

steps.p: Most wasted test budget comes from a few repeat mistakes. If you recognise one of these in your plan, fix it before you spend, because no amount of later analysis can rescue a badly designed test.
d: Too many variants|budget spread too thin
Moving goalposts|metric picked after the fact
Stopped early|noise taken for a winner
steps.say: Most wasted test budget comes from a few repeat mistakes. Look at the cards. Too many variants, so budget is spread too thin. No control, so there's nothing to compare with. Moving goalposts, where the metric is picked after the fact. Stopped early, so noise is taken for a winner. And not recorded, so the same test gets repeated later. If you see one of these in your plan, fix it before you spend, because no later analysis can rescue a badly designed test.

steps.p: A test is still advertising. Every variant must follow ad policy and local law, carry the required risk or age wording and avoid claims you cannot prove. Never test a misleading claim to "see if it works". Trading and gambling ads usually need platform authorization; check both before you run.

d.text: If a variant would break policy as a full campaign, it breaks policy as a test.

steps.say: A test is still advertising. Every variant must follow ad policy and local law, carry the required risk or age wording, and avoid claims you can't prove. Never test a misleading claim just to see if it works. Trading and gambling ads usually need platform authorization, so check both policy and law before you run. Read the warning: if a variant would break policy as a full campaign, it breaks policy as a test.

steps.h: A clean loss is still a result
steps.p: Most tests lose, and that is normal. A losing test that was set up cleanly still tells you something true about your market and saves you from spending more on a wrong idea. Record losses as carefully as wins.

d.s: They rule ideas out for good

steps.say: Most tests lose, and that's normal. A losing test that was set up cleanly still tells you something true about your market. It saves you from spending more on a wrong idea, and it rules that idea out for good. So clean losses are useful. Record your losses as carefully as your wins.

lessons.title: Sample size and patience
objectives: By the end you can explain why big gaps show up fast and small gaps need lots of data.
You can size a test budget in multiples of your target CPA.
You can account for learning phases, time patterns and late deposits before calling a winner.

steps.h: Enough data depends on the gap
steps.p: There is no single magic number of clicks. How much data you need depends on how big the difference is between your versions. Large gaps show up quickly. Small gaps need a lot of data, and some are too small to be worth chasing at all.
steps.say: There's no single magic number of clicks. How much data you need depends on how big the difference is between your versions. Large gaps show up quickly. Small gaps need a lot of data. And some gaps are so small they aren't worth chasing at all. Keep that idea in mind for the whole lesson: big gaps show fast, small gaps need large samples.

steps.p: Example: two landers, one converting at 2% and one at 4%. With about 1,000 clicks each you expect about 20 versus 40 conversions, and the rough ranges barely touch. If the gap is 2% versus 2.2%, the same clicks give 20 versus 22, which is pure noise.
steps.more: Using the rough range from lesson one: 20 gives about 11 to 29, and 40 gives about 27 to 53. They only touch at the edges. At 250 clicks, 5 (about 1 to 9) and 10 (about 4 to 16) overlap heavily. For a 10% relative gap like 2% versus 2.2%, you need tens of thousands of clicks per side before the ranges pull apart. Most small buyers cannot afford that, so they should hunt for bigger gaps instead.
steps.say: Let's look at the table. Example: two landers, one converting at two percent and one at four. With two hundred and fifty clicks each, you expect five versus ten, and the rough ranges overlap heavily, so it's not clear. With about one thousand clicks each, you expect twenty versus forty, and the ranges barely touch. Mostly clear. But two percent versus two point two percent on a thousand clicks gives twenty versus twenty two. That's pure noise. You'd need tens of thousands of clicks per side, so most small buyers should hunt for bigger gaps instead.

steps.h: Budget in multiples of target CPA
steps.p: A practical way to size a test is to give each variant a budget measured in your target cost per action. A common rough guide is two to three times the target CPA per variant before a final call. It varies by geo and vertical.

d.label: target CPA per variant before a final call
d.note: Rough guide, varies by geo and vertical.

steps.say: Here's a practical way to size a test. Give each variant a budget measured in your target C P A, cost per acquisition. The number on screen is three times. A common rough guide is two to three times the target C P A per variant before you make a final call. It varies by geo and vertical, so treat it as a starting point.

steps.p: Example: target cost per FTD is $25, you test 3 creatives, and you plan 3x target CPA for each. The test needs about $225. If your daily budget is $45, that is five days. Know this number before launch so you do not panic on day two.
steps.more: Check: $25 × 3 = $75 per variant. $75 × 3 variants = $225. $225 ÷ $45 per day = 5 days. Even at 3x, each variant may only have 2 to 4 FTDs if it performs near target, which is still a small count. That is why this budget is for spotting clear winners and clear losers, and why close calls go to a second, confirming round.
steps.say: Let's size one. Example: your target cost per F T D, first time deposit, is twenty five dollars. You test three creatives, and you plan three times target C P A for each. Twenty five times three is seventy five dollars per variant. Times three variants is two hundred and twenty five dollars. At forty five dollars a day, that's five days. Even then, each variant may only have two to four F T Ds, still a small count. So this budget spots clear winners and losers, and close calls go to a second, confirming round.

steps.p: Use the sizing rule from the slide above. Three creatives, 3 × target CPA each, target $25, and you want the test finished in 5 days. Enter the daily budget for the whole test.
steps.more: Answer: $45 a day. 3 creatives × 3 = 9 target CPAs. 9 × $25 = $225. $225 ÷ 5 days = $45 a day, $15 per creative. That is above half the target per ad set per day, so each one reaches the 2 × zero-FTD line in under 4 days.

steps.p: With a fixed budget, every extra variant gets less money and less data. Five creatives on $100 means $20 each, which may not buy a single FTD. Two or three variants with enough budget each will teach you more than many starved ones.
steps.say: With a fixed budget, every extra variant gets less money and less data. Compare the two sides. One hundred dollars across five ads is twenty dollars each. That's often zero or one F T D each, so the winner is picked by luck and you need a retest. One hundred dollars across two ads is fifty each. You get a few results each, the gap is easier to read, and your next step is clearer. Two or three well-funded variants teach you more than many starved ones.

steps.h: Use earlier signals while you wait
steps.p: When deposits are too rare to judge quickly, use a ladder. Screen creatives on early metrics that have lots of data, keep the ones that pass, and judge only the survivors on deposits. Early metrics can mislead, so always confirm with money before scaling.
steps.more: Early metrics mislead when an ad attracts curious clickers who never deposit. A shocking hook can win on CTR and lose on FTDs. That is why each step of the ladder is a filter, not a final verdict. The final call always uses the metric you are paid on.
d: Screen on hook rate or CTR
steps.say: When deposits are too rare to judge quickly, use a ladder. Follow the flow. Screen on hook rate or C T R, click through rate. Shortlist on cost per lead. Confirm on cost per F T D. And scale on R O I, return on investment. Each step is a filter, not a final verdict. Early metrics can mislead. A shocking hook can win on C T R and lose on F T Ds, because it attracts curious clickers who never deposit. So always confirm with money before scaling.

steps.p: Ad platforms need some conversions to learn who to show your ad to. While an ad set is learning, costs often swing more than usual, and big edits can restart learning. Give new ad sets room and batch your edits. Thresholds change; check the current platform help.
steps.more: Example only. Both ad sets start the same. The one left alone settles as the platform learns. The one edited every day keeps getting knocked back into learning, so its cost per lead never settles. Real accounts are noisier than this, but the pattern of frequent edits causing instability is common.

steps.p: Results change by hour and by day for reasons that have nothing to do with your ad. If your test only runs over a weekend or during a big football match, the result may not hold on a normal Tuesday.
d: Day of week|weekends can differ from weekdays
Time zone|ads may run while your geo sleeps
steps.say: Results change by hour and by day for reasons that have nothing to do with your ad. Look at the cards. Day of week, because weekends can differ from weekdays. Paydays, because month end can shift deposits. Events, like matches, holidays and elections. And time zone, because ads may run while your geo sleeps. If your test only runs over a weekend, or during a big football match, the result may not hold on a normal Tuesday.

steps.p: Many users join today and deposit days later. If you judge a test the evening it ends, the slower variant may look worse simply because its depositors have not acted yet. Leave a short wait after the test before the final read.

d.text: Example: a test ends on Friday. Read joins on Friday, but read FTDs again on Monday or Tuesday before deciding, once late depositors have had time to show up.

steps.p: Track each variant's spend, network-confirmed FTDs and rough range in one sheet, with the rule-card call beside it. Example on day 3 of a $25-target test: nothing has crossed a kill or scale line yet, so every call is Hold. Doing nothing on purpose is part of the method.

Hook C, forty five and zero, still under the fifty dollar kill line. Nothing has crossed a kill or scale line, so every call is hold. The final call comes at seventy five dollars each. steps.p: The rough range shrinks as conversions grow, but slowly. To halve the range you need about four times the data. This is why the first few results feel exciting and later ones feel dull: each extra result adds a little less certainty.
steps.more: Each bar is the rough range as a share of the count. 4 ± 4 is ±100%. 16 ± 8 is ±50%. 64 ± 16 is ±25%. 256 ± 32 is ±12.5%. Every time the count goes up four times, the range as a share halves.

At four results, the range is plus or minus one hundred percent. At sixteen, fifty percent. At sixty four, twenty five percent. At two hundred and fifty six, twelve and a half percent. That's why the first few results feel exciting and later ones feel dull. Each extra result adds a little less certainty.

steps.p: Run through these questions before you declare a winner. If any answer is no, keep the test running or plan a follow-up test to confirm what you think you saw.
d: Each variant reached its planned budget
Each has enough conversions to compare
Late conversions had time to arrive
The gap held for several days
steps.say: Before you declare a winner, run through these questions. Did each variant reach its planned budget? Does each have enough conversions to compare? Have late conversions had time to arrive? Did the gap hold for several days? And did nothing else change mid-test? If any answer is no, keep the test running, or plan a follow-up test to confirm what you think you saw.

steps.p: Impatience costs more than slow tests. These mistakes all end a test before the data can answer the question, so the money spent so far buys a guess instead of a result.
d: Too many variants|each one starved of data
Calling it on day 2|before the checkpoint
Reading FTDs the night it ends|late deposits missing
Raising budget to "speed up"|changes what you are testing
steps.say: Impatience costs more than slow tests. Look at these common mistakes. Too many variants, each one starved of data. Calling it on day two, before the checkpoint. Reading F T Ds the night it ends, with late deposits missing. Editing mid-test, so learning resets and data mixes. And raising the budget to speed up, which changes what you're testing. Each one ends a test before the data can answer, so the money spent buys a guess instead of a result.

steps.p: Patience costs money, so plan for it. Set the test budget aside before launch and treat it as tuition. If you cannot afford to finish a test, run fewer variants or ask a smaller question instead of stopping halfway and guessing.

takeaways: Big gaps show up with modest data; small gaps need far more than most small budgets allow.
Size tests in multiples of target CPA per variant, and run fewer variants on small budgets.
Respect learning phases, day and payday patterns, and late deposits before the final read.

lessons.title: Kill, hold and scale rules
objectives: By the end you can write a kill rule ladder measured in multiples of target CPA.
You can check tracking and offer status before any rule fires.
You can set scale rules for winners as well as kill rules for losers.

steps.h: Decide your rules before you spend
steps.p: When money is burning, judgment gets worse. Kill rules are decisions you make calmly before launch: at this spend, with these numbers, I stop. Written rules protect you from hope, fear and the urge to give a loser one more day.

d.s: Written before launch, applied without debate

steps.say: When money is burning, judgment gets worse. Kill rules are decisions you make calmly before launch: at this spend, with these numbers, I stop. Rules first, money second. They're written before launch and applied without debate. Written rules protect you from hope, from fear, and from the urge to give a loser one more day.

steps.p: Dchessking on the habit that keeps a weak ad set from quietly eating a whole week of budget. It is simple, and it only works if you write it down before the campaign goes live.

steps.p: Lagging metrics such as cost per FTD are what you get paid on, but they arrive late and in small numbers. Leading metrics such as CTR and cost per join arrive early and in volume. Good rules use leading metrics for warnings and lagging ones for final calls.

Cost per join|middle: is the funnel working?
Cost per FTD|late: does it make money?
steps.say: There are two kinds of metrics. Lagging metrics, like cost per F T D, first time deposit, are what you get paid on, but they arrive late and in small numbers. Leading metrics arrive early and in volume. Look at the cards. C T R, click through rate, asks: is the ad stopping people? C P C, cost per click: is traffic affordable? Cost per join: is the funnel working? And cost per F T D: does it make money? Good rules use leading metrics for warnings and lagging ones for final calls.

steps.p: Example: target cost per FTD is $25. Ad set A has spent $50 with 0 FTDs but 40 joins. The ladder says kill at 2x with zero FTDs. Before you do, check the plumbing, because 40 joins with no deposits can mean a broken postback.

steps.h: Before you kill, check the plumbing
steps.p: A rule should never fire on broken data. Before you kill anything with zero conversions, spend two minutes confirming the zero is real. Many apparent losers turn out to be winners with a broken postback or a paused offer.

Offer link works on a phone

steps.p: Holding means leaving an ad set alone while you gather more data or test new creative beside it. Scaling means adding budget. Only scale when results are clear and stable, because scaling a noisy winner usually buys you its average result.

a.title: Hold when
items: CPA above target, under the kill line

steps.say: Hold and scale mean different things. Holding means leaving an ad set alone while you gather data or test new creative beside it. Scaling means adding budget. Look at the left: hold when there are fewer than three F T Ds, when C P A is above target but under the kill line, when a recent edit reset learning, or when late deposits are still arriving. On the right: scale with three or more confirmed F T Ds, C P A at point eight times target or less, at least seventy two hours running, and room in the offer cap. Scaling a noisy winner usually buys you its average result.

steps.p: When you scale, move in steps and watch what happens. The starting rule is to raise budget by 20% at a time and wait at least 48 hours before the next step, which must be earned again. Big jumps can reset learning and push costs up. It varies by platform and account.
steps.more: Example: an ad set at $50 a day goes to $60, then $72, then about $86, with at least 48 hours between steps. That is three steps to raise it about 73%. Each step needs CPA since the last step still at or under 0.8 × target. If CPA since the step stays above target for 48 hours, go back to the last good budget.

steps.p: Rules only work if you follow them. These four traps are how most buyers end up ignoring their own rules. Name the trap when you notice it, and let the written rule win.

Favourite ad|you made it, so you protect it

steps.p: Kill rules get the attention, but winners need rules as well. Decide in advance how fast you scale, when you duplicate and when you stop. Without them, buyers often over-scale a winner and give back the profit it made.

lessons.title: Dashboards and weekly reviews
objectives: By the end you can build a small dashboard where every column leads to a decision.
You can break totals down by segment and read cohorts fairly.
You can run a weekly review with a fixed agenda and a decisions log.

steps.h: Data is only useful when you read it
steps.p: Most buyers collect plenty of numbers and read very few of them. A simple dashboard and a fixed weekly review turn scattered numbers into decisions. The aim is fewer, clearer numbers that you read the same way every time.
steps.say: Most buyers collect plenty of numbers and read very few of them. A simple dashboard and a fixed weekly review turn scattered numbers into decisions. The aim is fewer, clearer numbers, read every week, with the same layout and the same questions. That's what this lesson builds.

steps.p: Good reporting has three layers: a daily check for problems, a weekly review for decisions and a monthly look at strategy. Mixing them up causes trouble, such as changing your whole strategy after one bad day.
d: Weekly|about an hour: kill, hold, scale
steps.say: Good reporting has three layers. Look at the cards. Daily: five minutes, asking is anything broken? Weekly: about an hour, deciding kill, hold or scale. Monthly: strategy, meaning geos, offers and budget. Mixing them up causes trouble, like changing your whole strategy after one bad day. Keep each question at its own layer.

steps.p: Start with a small set of columns, one row per campaign or ad set. Every number should lead to a decision. If a column never changes what you do, remove it. The figures below are an example.
steps.say: Start with a small set of columns, one row per campaign or ad set. Look at the table, with example figures. Spend, from the ad platform, one thousand two hundred dollars. C T R, click through rate, clicks divided by impressions. Cost per join, spend divided by joins. F T Ds, first time deposits, from the network: forty. Cost per F T D: thirty dollars. Revenue, F T Ds times payout: one thousand six hundred. And R O I, return on investment: thirty three percent. Every number should lead to a decision. If a column never changes what you do, remove it.

steps.h: The dashboard with a decision column
steps.p: Example: the core columns per ad set, plus one more: the rule-card call. Target $30, payout $40, network-confirmed FTDs. When every row ends in a decision, the weekly review takes minutes instead of an hour of staring at numbers.

A S two: three hundred and ninety for thirteen, exactly thirty dollars. Keep. A S three: three hundred and ninety for nine, forty three thirty three, over the kill line past three times target. Kill. When every row ends in a decision, the review takes minutes.

Revenue is one thousand six hundred, so profit is four hundred. R O I is profit divided by spend, so about thirty three percent. And use the network's confirmed F T Ds, since platform numbers can differ.

steps.p: A total can look fine while one part loses money. Example: the campaign shows 33% ROI overall. Split by geo and one geo is at 80% ROI while the other loses money. Always break totals down by geo, ad set and creative before deciding.

Moving Geo B's budget to Geo A could lift the total, if Geo A can take more spend at a similar cost. So always break totals down by geo, ad set and creative before deciding.

steps.h: Cohorts: give each week fair credit
steps.p: Deposits from this week's spend keep arriving next week. If you compare this week's spend only with this week's FTDs, recent weeks look worse than they are. A cohort view links each FTD back to the week the user arrived.
steps.more: Example. People who joined in week 1 produced 8 FTDs on their first day and 25 by their seventh day. If you judged week 1 on day one, cost per FTD would look about three times worse than it really was. Judge each week only once most of its depositors have had time to arrive, and compare weeks at the same age.
steps.say: Deposits from this week's spend keep arriving next week. Compare this week's spend only with this week's F T Ds, and recent weeks look worse than they are. A cohort view links each F T D back to the week the user arrived. Look at the lines in this example. Week one joiners produced eight F T Ds on day one and twenty five by day seven. Judge week one on day one, and cost per F T D looks about three times worse. So compare weeks at the same age.

steps.p: Run the same agenda every week, at the same time. A fixed order stops you from jumping to the exciting parts and skipping the dull checks that often matter most, such as whether network numbers match your tracker.
steps.say: Run the same agenda every week, at the same time. Follow the flow. Reconcile numbers. Review by segment. Apply rules. Read finished tests. Plan next tests. And log decisions. A fixed order stops you jumping to the exciting parts and skipping the dull checks that often matter most, like whether network numbers match your tracker.

steps.p: Your ad platform, tracker and network will rarely agree exactly. Small steady gaps are normal because of attribution windows and timing. Big or growing gaps mean something is broken. Judge profit on the network's confirmed numbers and use platform numbers for optimisation signals.

steps.p: Write down every important decision with the date and the reason. After a few months the log becomes your own playbook. You can see which rules worked, which tests you already ran and why a campaign changed.

steps.p: Weekly reviews are where slow problems show up. Creative fatigue is a common one: frequency climbs, CTR slides and cost per result rises over a few weeks. One day of data hides it. A weekly view makes it obvious.

steps.p: A dashboard can make you feel informed while hiding the very problem you need to see. These mistakes are common because each one makes the numbers look calmer or better than they are.

steps.p: The review is where people fool themselves most, because they want the numbers to say something. These habits keep you honest, especially when a campaign you love is fading or one you doubted is working.

steps.h: One hour a week pays for itself
steps.p: One focused hour a week often saves more money than any new trick. It catches broken tracking, stops slow losers and finds the winners that deserve more budget. Book it in your calendar and protect it like a meeting with your biggest client.

It makes the test unfair, nothing else
quiz.why: A translated ad must say the same honest things, including risk warnings. Dropping them makes a different, non-compliant ad.

lessons.say_intro: This lesson puts everything together. You'll follow one example creative test day by day, from the test card to the logged decision, so your first real test isn't the first time you've seen one done.
lessons.say_outro: You've run one full test from card to logged decision, applied the rule card at each checkpoint, and separated the budget call from what the test actually proved. Your task: write a full test card for your next test, with the payout, target, break-even, kill lines, scale line, daily budget and the day you'll make the final call. Now take the quiz.

exam.q: Two ads each spent $40. Ad A has 2 FTDs, Ad B has 1. Target CPA is $25. What is the best next step?
options: Kill B now, it is half as good
Keep both running to the planned checkpoint: neither has 3 FTDs and the gap could be noise
Move all budget to A immediately
Scale A because its CPA is under target
exam.why: Neither has 3 FTDs, so neither can scale or keep, and both have conversions with spend under 3 × target, so neither is killed. 2 and 1 have overlapping rough ranges. Hold both.

exam.q: You spent $60, got 0 FTDs, target CPA $25. Your ladder kills at 2x with zero FTDs. Joins look normal. What do you do first?
options: Raise the budget to get more data
Confirm on the network dashboard and check the postback, then apply the rule
Change the creative and keep going
exam.why: $60 is 2.4x target, so the rule applies, but only after confirming the zero is real.

exam.q: You want to know whether a Swahili voiceover beats English in Kenya. Which setup is cleanest?
options: Same video, two voiceovers, separate ad sets with equal budgets, same audience and start time
Swahili video to one audience, English to a different audience
Both voiceovers plus a new lander in one ad set
Run English this week and Swahili next week
exam.why: Only the voiceover changes, budgets are equal and timing is the same, so the result points to the voiceover.

exam.q: Target CPA $20, 4 variants, 3x target per variant, $60 a day. How long does the test take?
Test day 5: control $75 with 1 FTD, variant $75 with 4 FTDs. Target $25, payout $35. What are the calls?
options: Kill the control (CPA $75 over the $35 kill line at 3 × spend); scale the variant +20% and plan a confirming round
exam.why: Control: spend at 3 × target, CPA over the kill line, so kill. Variant: $18.75 is 0.75 × target with 4 FTDs, so scale. The rough ranges overlap, so confirm the lesson in a second round.

exam.q: An ad set had its best ever day yesterday and now has 3 FTDs at 0.7 × target after 2 days. A teammate wants to triple the budget today. What do you advise?
options: Wait until it has run at least 72 hours, then raise 20% and wait 48 hours before the next step
exam.why: One great day often regresses to the mean, and the starting scale rule needs 72 hours running, then +20% steps at least 48 hours apart.

exam.q: Weekly totals: $2,000 spend, 50 FTDs, $45 payout. What is ROI?
This week looks worse than last week on cost per FTD, but it ended yesterday. What is the most likely reason to wait before judging?
options: The platform hides data for a week
Late deposits from this week's joiners have not arrived yet
exam.why: Conversion delay means recent cohorts are incomplete. Compare weeks at the same age.

exam.q: You screened 10 hooks on CTR and found one with double the usual CTR. What is the right next step?
options: Kill the other nine and stop testing
Shortlist it and confirm on cost per lead and cost per FTD before scaling
exam.why: Leading metrics screen ideas, but a high CTR can attract curious clickers who never deposit. Confirm with money.

exam.q: Your automated rule paused an ad set at 3am for 0 results after $30. In the morning the network shows 2 FTDs from it. What went wrong and what do you fix?
options: The rule used tracker data that missed conversions; fix the postback and review the rule
exam.why: Rules only work on accurate data. Fix the data feed first, then decide whether the rule thresholds still make sense.
